content: 1. The CDC, along with its planners and content experts, has disclosed that they do not have any financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. 2. Presentations will not include any discussion of the off-label use of a product or investigational use of a product. 3. The CDC does not accept commercial support. 4. In 1990, the CDC published guidelines for investigating clusters of health events, referred to as the 1990 Guidelines. 5. The 1990 Guidelines did not focus on any specific disease but considered noninfectious diseases, injuries, birth defects, and previously unrecognized syndromes or illnesses. 6. Many state, local, and tribal health departments have used the 1990 Guidelines as a foundation for developing and implementing protocols to investigate suspected cancer clusters, employing a four-step approach: initial response, assessment, major feasibility study, and etiologic investigation. 7. Since the publication of the 1990 Guidelines, there has been continued attention to suspected cancer clusters nationwide, prompting the CDC to publish additional details on the role of the guidelines in responding specifically to cancer clusters. 8. Since 1990, significant advancements have been made in data resources, investigative techniques, and analytic/statistical methods, with valuable lessons learned from both largeand small-scale cancer cluster investigations. 9. This report enhances the 1990 Guidelines by focusing specifically on cancer cluster investigations. 10. The guidance provided in this report addresses additional subject areas deemed important by epidemiologists from state and local health departments. 11. These additional subject areas include communication strategies, resources for data, and the use of epidemiologic and spatial statistical methods. 12. Useful websites, a resource not available in 1990, have been added to the updated guidelines. 13. The four-step process from the 1990 Guidelines has been retained, with additional details provided. 14. Public health personnel in state and local health departments can use these updated guidelines to develop a systematic approach when responding to inquiries about suspected cancer clusters in residential or community settings. 15. Additionally, these guidelines may be helpful to a broader community of responders and epidemiologists concerned with such inquiries. 16. These types of inquiries are often initiated by community members or medical professionals concerned about what appears to be an unusually high number of diagnosed cancer cases in a particular community, workplace, family, or school. 17. Upon receiving an initial inquiry, health department personnel should respond promptly to the caller's concerns, gather relevant information about the cancer cases, make a professional judgment on the likelihood that the reported situation represents an actual increase in cancer cases beyond what is expected in a particular population, and determine whether further investigation is warranted. 18. If appropriate, health department personnel will need to provide resources for investigating the suspected cluster, working with and involving community members as much as possible throughout the process. 19. In March 2010, the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) and the CDC convened a workgroup to revise the 1990 Guidelines. 20. The workgroup consisted of public health professionals selected by the leadership of CSTE's Environmental Epidemiology Subcommittee and by the CDC's National Center for Environmental Health's Division of Environmental Hazards and Health Effects. 21. CSTE and CDC selected workgroup members with experience in responding to cancer cluster inquiries from communities and managing cancer cluster investigations. 22. 23. Additionally, CDC workgroup members included representatives from CDC organizations typically called upon to assist in cancer cluster investigations, such as the National Center for Environmental Health, the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, and the National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion's Division of Cancer Prevention and Control. 24. CDC risk communication and statistical specialists, as well as epidemiologists from academic institutions experienced in cancer cluster investigations, also participated in the workgroup. 25. 26. Through regularly scheduled conference calls and meetings from March 2010 to May 2011, the workgroup identified areas that warranted changes from the 1990 Guidelines and sources of new information to incorporate into the revised guidelines. 27. For these topics, medical librarians at the CDC Public Health Library and Information Center conducted a comprehensive review of the published, peer-reviewed literature. 28. To identify articles related to community cancer clusters, librarians conducted a structured literature search using multiple databases, including PubMed, MEDLINE, and CAB. 29. English-language peer-reviewed articles published between 1969 and 2010 were searched using medical subject heading (MeSH) terms such as cluster analysis, cancer cluster, neoplasm, environmental illness, and non-occupational diseases. 30. Through this process, 166 articles were identified. 31. Additionally, workgroup members recommended 26 publications, including those on communications and statistical analysis, as well as non-scientific publications related to cancer clusters, and three unpublished cancer cluster investigation reports relevant to topics addressed in the guidelines. 32. All articles and reports were reviewed by the workgroup members. 33. Regarding topics for which no new published evidence was available, expert opinion was sought from workgroup members. 34. In October 2010, an in-person meeting of the workgroup was held to begin writing the revised guidelines. 35. In addition to convening a technical workgroup, CSTE sent a survey to all state and territorial epidemiologists to assess the needs of public health professionals when responding to cancer cluster concerns, in order to direct the focus and content of the guidelines. 36. The survey included questions about the most common activities states engage in when addressing a cancer cluster inquiry and what type of information would be useful. 37. This survey identified areas, such as communications, resources for data, and epidemiologic methods, in which more details would be useful. 38. After discussion, review, and incorporation of the findings from the survey, the workgroup decided to retain and update the four-step approach first described in the 1990 Guidelines. 39. Updates included incorporating new technological advances, such as the use of the Internet and websites, for information on relevant data resources, statistical tests, and mapping techniques, as well as lessons learned from recent cancer cluster investigations. 40. One important update is the emphasis on the importance of developing a robust working relationship with the community as soon as possible, including clear two-way communication and transparency in all aspects of the response process, while maintaining scientific rigor. 41. The revised guidelines address questions about the availability of data, limitations associated with understanding cancer clusters, and decision-making about the extent to which inquiries can be followed up. 42. For specificity, the revised guidelines are limited in scope to include only those situations in which a health department responds to an inquiry about a suspected cancer cluster in a residential or community setting. 43. These guidelines do not address workplace cancer clusters or those related to medical treatment, such as cancers associated with pharmaceuticals. 44. Workplace or occupational clusters and medically related clusters each present unique sets of circumstances, have unique and clearly defined populations at risk, and generally call for specific investigative methods, agencies, and partnerships. 45. Similarly, these guidelines do not discuss diseases other than cancer that persons might suspect have occurred in clusters in their communities. 46. However, some of the principles of risk communication, data analysis, and community involvement discussed in this report might be applicable to non-cancer cluster investigations as well. 47. Finally, the revised guidelines do not address routine surveillance conducted by cancer registries and programs to assess trends.
